CASE PRESENTATION
A 26- year- old woman with SPS was referred to our 
acute pain service for excruciating bilateral hand 
and truncal spasms and severe pain unresponsive 
to conventional first- line and second- line therapies. 
This occurred weeks following a clinical diagnosis 
of SPS, occurring on a background of controlled 
Addison’s disease, systemic lupus erythematosus 
and Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. Anti- GAD65 anti-
bodies were elevated in the serum (38.6 U/mL, refer-
ence range <5 U/mL) but were consistently negative 
in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Extended panels of 
autoimmune and paraneoplastic antineuronal anti-
bodies, including amphiphysin, glycine receptor, 
dipeptidyl- peptidase- like protein 6 (DPPX) and 
N- methyl- D- aspartate (NMDA) receptor antibodies, 
were also negative in the serum and CSF, although 
at the height of her illness the patient had a CSF 
lymphocytosis which normalised as the patient’s 
symptoms improved. The patient had been diag-
nosed during a recent admission to the neurology 
unit where she was treated with high- dose intrave-
nous steroids, IVIG, plasmapheresis and rituximab. 
She was discharged with 2 mg clonazepam four 
times daily, 50 mg baclofen two times daily, 25 µg 
clonidine three times daily, 400 mg gabapentin four 
times daily, 100 mg immediate release tapentadol 
three times daily and 1 g paracetamol three times 
daily for symptomatic treatment (figure 1). Four 
days after discharge, the patient re- presented after 
five episodes of debilitating truncal spasms, rigidity 
and a baseline pain score of 8 out of 10. T riggers 
for her spasms included anxiety and anger, as well 
as rapid movements, upper limb muscle tension and 
notably, inadequately controlled pain. As such, the 
patient was referred to the acute pain service in 
order to optimise her pain control with a view to 
avoid spasms.
Early in her second admission, the patient was 
given an additional 50 µg dose of clonidine and 
25 mg baclofen at night for improved nocturnal 
control of symptoms. With pain unchanged on day 
three of admission, as well as three salvos of severe 
spasms, clonazepam dosing was increased from four 
to five times daily in conjunction with 100 mg oral

tramadol immediate release four times daily. Despite this, baseline 
pain scores did not improve, and with nine episodes of spasms 
over the next 2 days, she was given sodium valproate 250 mg 
two times daily. With continued refractory pain on day seven 
of her admission and having achieved demonstrably insufficient 
pain relief on both opioid and non- opioid analgesia, she was 
started on an intravenous ketamine patient- controlled analgesia 
(PCA) with 10 mg of ketamine per patient bolus as well as addi-
tional intravenous nurse- administered boluses of 5 mg ketamine 
in the case that the PCA dose was insufficient. Our patient was 
educated on appropriate use of the ketamine PCA and instructed 
to use it early in the progression of an episode prior to migration 
to her trunk. On her next spasm, the patient used the ketamine 
PCA and received an additional 5 mg bolus at the earliest onset 
of her spasm, which was followed by painless termination of the 
episode within 30 s. Due to the possible effectiveness of ketamine 
in avoiding worsening spasms, perhaps through indirect means 
of controlling acute pain, nurse- administered ketamine boluses 
were increased from 5 to 10 mg. While the ketamine PCA was 
able to provide transient pain relief and cessation of an episode, 
there was continued inadequate baseline pain control. As 
such, 100 mg of sustained release tapentadol was added to the 
patient’s regimen two times daily. Shortly after this amendment, 
the patient experienced a 35- minute excruciating spasm, which 
could not be terminated immediately with ketamine. It was later 
decided that all doses of immediate and sustained release tapen-
tadol and tramadol be ceased due to documented potential for 
exacerbating SPS.10
Due to the lack of sustainability of ketamine PCA for pain 
management and a paucity of evidence- based options that had 
not already been attempted, it was decided that the patient 
be trialled on a magnesium sulfate (MgSO 4) infusion using 
a modified hospital- based pre- eclampsia seizure prophylaxis 
protocol. As such, the patient was started on a MgSO 4 infusion 
via her previously placed peripherally inserted central cath-
eter (PICC line). A loading dose of 4 g was administered over 
15 min, followed by a maintenance dose of 2 g/hour for the next 
24 hours. During this time, the patient received regular obser -
vations and blood magnesium measurements with a therapeutic 
magnesium range of 1.7–3.5 mmol/L. The patient reported mild 
facial flushing during the infusion which did not limit therapy; 
however, the infusion was temporarily ceased due to a serum 
magnesium above the therapeutic range in the absence of overt 
magnesium toxicity. Reflexes remained at baseline. Calcium 
gluconate was administered with improvement of serum magne-
sium and she was given MgSO4 infusion at half the maintenance 
dose used previously (1 g/hour) with no reported adverse effects. 
After a total of 72 hours on the infusion with minimal noticeable 
change in the patient’s clinical profile, the infusion was ceased.
In an effort to transition our patient to more sustainable anal-
gesia for discharge preparation, the ketamine PCA was replaced 
with ketamine wafers and immediate release oral oxycodone for 
spasm termination alone. It was also recognised by the patient 
that manual massage of the limbs prior to truncal involvement of

a spasm had the effect of reducing pain and likelihood of spasm 
migration. As such, this was included in the patient’s acute spasm 
management. On the patient’s next spasm onset, she was admin-
istered 5 mg oxycodone as well as a 50 mg ketamine wafer in 
conjunction with manual limb massage and 10 mg buccal midaz-
olam, which resulted in avoidance of progression of the acute 
episode. With growing concerns expressed by the patient of 
excessive drowsiness, clonazepam dosing was gradually reduced 
to 1.5 mg three times daily with plans to further reduce the dose 
after discharge. Furthermore, in order to address psychological 
components of pain, chronic disease and triggering of spasms, 
the patient was offered hospital mental health services and 
was recommended community psychological services. Due to 
ongoing reasonably well- controlled pain and spasms, the patient 
was transferred for inpatient acute rehabilitation which also 
allowed facilitation of in- home caring services.
OUTCOME AND FOLLOW-UP
The patient successfully completed inpatient acute rehabilita -
tion and has continued follow- up as an outpatient. Throughout 
the follow- up period of 6 months, the patient has experienced 
very occasional minor spasms, with significantly improved pain 
control and quality of life. During her follow- up, her clonaz-
epam dosage was weaned to 1 mg daily and she no longer 
requires oxycodone, valproate, gabapentin or clonidine and 
rarely requires ibuprofen or paracetamol. The patient is also on 
50 mg baclofen three times daily and is in the process of grad-
ually reducing this dose. The patient has been able to control 
the onset of acute spasms with 50 mg of sublingual ketamine 
in conjunction with manual limb massage, and seldom requires 
buccal midazolam for spasm termination. She continues to 
manage her multiple autoimmune conditions with azathioprine, 
thyroxine, hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone.

Our patient had been taking regular clonazepam 
and baclofen from her first admission, which appeared to have 
little effect. Furthermore, the patient received both IVIG and 
plasmapheresis during her previous admission and was on 
weekly rituximab therapy. Despite exhaustion of both first- line 
and second- line therapies, the patient continued to experience 
regular painful spasms with uncontrolled pain lasting beyond the 
episodes themselves.
There is minimal evidence to suggest how patients with unre-
mitting pain should be managed beyond first- line and second- 
line disease- modifying therapies for SPS. Reports of SPS patients 
with pain as the predominant symptom have suggested the 
use of opioids including regular morphine, which was largely 
avoided here due to the likelihood of dependence in a young 
woman.8 The patient was however prescribed immediate release

oral oxycodone in the event of a pain exacerbation that would 
precipitate further spasms in an attempt to transition her to the 
community setting. As such, a multifaceted approach to pain 
management was used in order to address central and peripheral 
pain pathways including that of the opioid, serotonergic, adren-
ergic, GABAergic and glutaminergic pathways. We also consid-
ered inflammation and its role in the patient’s presentation, with 
the patient taking regular celecoxib as well as hydrocortisone, 
azathioprine and hydroxychloroquine to control her additional 
autoimmune conditions. Despite such attempts to manage our 
patient’s pain, the episodes of excruciating spasms continued 
and, if anything, were increasingly prolonged. As such, we 
reviewed the literature on analgesics in SPS, which revealed that

there had been documented cases of serotonin- norepinephrine 
reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) exacerbating SPS with subsequent 
clinical improvements in patients with cessation of the SNRI. 10 
This supports the role of the noradrenergic system in SPS, which 
may explain the exacerbation of symptoms with SNRIs, stress 
and anxiety and clinical improvement in SPS with the alpha-2 
adrenoreceptor agonist clonidine.9 It is notable that the patient 
had an extended spasm shortly after she was started on sustained 
release tapentadol, which is known to significantly increase 
extracellular norepinephrine. Subsequently, both tramadol and 
tapentadol were discontinued due to their known SNRI mecha-
nisms of action.
In an effort to further address the rigidity and spasms contrib-
uting to ongoing pain, attention was given to sourcing sustain-
able long- term therapies. Magnesium sulfate has been used for 
the prevention of seizures in pre- eclampsia, and more recently, 
has gained attention for its potentiating effects on periopera-
tive analgesia and muscle relaxation. 13 While magnesium is not 
itself an analgesic, it has been shown to enhance the analgesic 
actions of more established agents by abrogating somatic, auto-
nomic and endocrine reflexes provoked by noxious stimuli. 14 
Furthermore, magnesium acts to increase muscle relaxation via 
its activity as a presynaptic calcium channel blocker, thereby 
reducing acetylcholine release to diminish muscle fibre excit-
ability.15 It is unclear whether magnesium had any significant 
effect in this patient due to confounding variables in the patient’s 
care. Further research into the role of magnesium supplementa-
tion in SPS may be warranted.
Our patient appeared to have significant responses to 
ketamine, although transient, where other therapies were 
ineffective at providing sufficient analgesia. It appeared that 
ketamine boluses had the occasional effect of avoiding truncal 
migration of an episode when taken early in the progression of 
a spasm, likely secondary to acute pain cessation. Ketamine has 
been used previously for procedural sedation in SPS as reported 
in a single case report. However, this is the first documentation 
of ketamine for analgesia in SPS.16 The success of this agent gave 
rise to additional issues when attempting to transition analgesia 
to the community setting with concerns regarding risks of inap-
propriate use and dependency. As a result, we transitioned the 
patient from PCA intravenous ketamine to sublingual ketamine 
wafers. The patient could continue to use the wafers in conjunc-
tion with oral oxycodone, buccal midazolam and manual limb 
massages in the patient rehabilitation and outpatient settings.
In conclusion, we present the case of a woman with SPS expe-
riencing refractory pain. We report the novel use of magnesium 
sulfate infusions and ketamine which may provide analgesia, 
spasm prophylaxis and early termination of exacerbations.
